content: In inorganic chemistry, a nitrate is defined as a salt derived from nitric acid, containing an ion composed of one nitrogen atom and three oxygen atoms (NO₃⁻). In the context of organic chemistry, nitrates refer to esters of nitric acid and various alcohols. The nitrate ion is the conjugate base of nitric acid and consists of a central nitrogen atom surrounded by three identical oxygen atoms arranged in a trigonal planar geometry. This ion carries a formal charge of negative one, with each oxygen atom bearing a charge of -2/3 and the nitrogen atom carrying a charge of +1. Nitrates are often used as a classic example of resonance, as the three canonical structures of the nitrate ion resonate with one another. Nearly all inorganic nitrate salts are highly soluble in water under standard temperature and pressure conditions. In organic chemistry, a nitrate functional group has the general chemical formula RONO₂, where R represents any organic residue. These compounds are formed as esters of nitric acid and alcohols through a process called nitroxylation. Examples include methyl nitrate, which is produced by the reaction of methanol and nitric acid, the nitrate of tartaric acid, and the compound commonly referred to as nitroglycerin, though its name is technically a misnomer. It is important to distinguish nitrates (NO₃⁻) from nitrites (NO₂⁻), which are salts of nitrous acid. Organic compounds containing the nitro functional group, which has a similar formula and structure to the nitrate ion except that one of the oxygen atoms is replaced by an organic group (R), are classified as nitro compounds. In freshwater or estuarine systems near land, nitrate levels can sometimes become elevated to concentrations that are harmful to aquatic life. Although nitrate is significantly less toxic than ammonia or nitrite, concentrations exceeding 30 ppm can inhibit growth, impair immune function, and induce stress in certain aquatic species. However, due to methodological issues in past acute nitrate toxicity studies, the extent of nitrate toxicity remains a topic of ongoing scientific debate. Excess nitrate concentrations in aquatic systems are often attributed to surface runoff from agricultural or landscaped areas that have been treated with excessive amounts of nitrate-based fertilizers. Elevated nitrate levels can also promote algal blooms, which, when nutrients such as potassium, phosphate, or nitrate become limiting, may lead to eutrophication. This process can result in water anoxia and other ecosystem changes, favoring certain groups of organisms over others. Consequently, because nitrates contribute to total dissolved solids, they are widely used as an indicator of water quality. Nitrates are also a by-product of septic systems. They are naturally occurring chemicals that remain after the decomposition of animal or human waste. Groundwater resources in watersheds with a high density of septic systems can be affected by nitrate contamination. Septic systems leach nitrates into groundwater or aquifers, which can then supply nearby bodies of water. Lakes that depend on groundwater are particularly susceptible to nitrate contamination through this process, often experiencing nitrification as a result.
